comment: The table of std.heap, the allocator of the runtime (std/heap.ft), for the rules of D10.9.
A row name gives the rule of D10.9 that the row breaks: rule 1 is no reuse of dead
storage, rule 2 the result of a read of dead storage, rule 4 `invalid release`, rule 5
`out of memory` and rule 6 the range of a call that changes a mapping, with the limit of
the holes that the give-back makes. A std module is
not part of the build of a test program, so the md5 guard reads the copy of the module in
the standard root of the debug preset, and the build copies it there itself. The compiler
binary keeps the allocator that its build gave it. The first stage runs the run tests of
the release rule in test/lang, and the second the module tests of the allocator in
test/fort. The table runs in the VM with the default runner after `tools/vm configure`

stages.name: the run tests of the release rule
stages.command: python3 test/lang/run_tests.py --fort build/Linux/debug/fort --std-dir build/Linux/debug/std --cc /usr/bin/clang --target x86_64-linux-gnu --timeout 600 run/pointers/01 run/pointers/02 run/errors/04 run/errors/05 run/stdlib/087 run/stdlib/157 run/stdlib/18

stages.name: the module tests of the allocator
stages.command: python3 test/lang/run_tests.py --root test/fort --fort build/Linux/debug/fort --std-dir build/Linux/debug/std --timeout 1500 -j 2 heap_test heap_segments_test heap_full_test heap_holes_test

mutations.what: the next allocation takes the storage of the newest allocation when a `del` released it
the frontier stays, so each large allocation and each small chunk takes the same chunks
the next small allocation starts at the last granule of the one before it
a give-back drops the pages of dead storage that a read can still reach, so the read gives zero bytes
the give-back of a huge allocation drops pages that a read can still reach
`drop` does not test the live bit of a small allocation: an address inside an allocation and the start of a dead one release
an address inside the first granule of a small allocation releases it
an address inside the first chunk of a large allocation releases it
the start of a later chunk of a large allocation releases that chunk
a released large allocation keeps its table words, so a second `drop` releases it again
`drop` looks at the newest mapping only, so an allocation of an older one never releases
an address inside a huge allocation releases it
a released huge allocation keeps its record, so a second `drop` releases it again
a small chunk that went back keeps its table word, so a `drop` of an address in it reads state that nothing can access
`take` rounds a size above the limit up, which is an integer overflow and no `out of memory`
`can_take` rounds a size above the limit up, which is an integer overflow and no refusal
a mapping that the system refused is the storage of an allocation
a large allocation takes one chunk more than its segment has left
an allocation of each chunk of a segment asks a segment for it, which holds one fewer
a give-back takes a unit that holds a live allocation
a give-back takes the units that hold the state of a small chunk with live allocations
mutations.old:
u64 mut unit = STATE_UNITS;
    while (unit < limit) {

mutations.what: the open chunk goes back when its last allocation dies, and the next allocation takes storage of it
a give-back makes hole 8193
the give-back that makes hole 8192 does not run
at the limit, a give-back that makes no new hole does not run
the allocator does not count the hole of a give-back
a give-back that joins two holes keeps the count of the holes
mutations.old:
// The run joins the hole before it and the hole after it.
        holes -= 1;
mutations.new:
// The run joins the hole before it and the hole after it.
        holes -= 0;

mutations.what: a dead large allocation whose storage stays gets the table word of a range that nothing can access
the give-back of a small chunk makes hole 8193
the allocator does not count the hole of a small chunk that goes back
the give-back of a small chunk does not count the hole inside the chunk, so it does not run at the limit
the give-back of a small chunk after a hole counts a new hole
the give-back of a small chunk before a hole counts a new hole, so it does not run at the limit
the first allocation unit of a segment stands after a hole
the last allocation unit below the frontier stands before a hole
the give-back of a small chunk sets the count of the holes to 0
the release of a huge allocation unmaps its mapping, so a later mapping can take its address range
a give-back of units or of a large allocation tells the system to drop no page, so the process keeps the pages of dead storage
mutations.old:
libc.madvise(cast(&h->words[at], void*), len, libc.MADV_DISCARD);
    return true;

mutations.what: the release of a huge allocation tells the system to drop no page, so the process keeps the pages of dead storage
a small chunk whose give-back the system refused stays a small chunk, so a later `drop` reads state that nothing can access
a claim whose storage the system refused moves the frontier, so the program gets storage that it cannot access
mutations.new:
libc.mprotect(cast(&h->words[first << CHUNK_WORDS_SHIFT], void*),
                  count << CHUNK_BYTES_SHIFT, libc.PROT_READ | libc.PROT_WRITE);

mutations.what: a new segment whose top table the system refused becomes the current segment, so the allocator writes a table that nothing can access
mutations.new: libc.mprotect(cast(r, void*), ONE << UNIT_BYTES_SHIFT, libc.PROT_READ | libc.PROT_WRITE);

mutations.what: a new segment whose top table the system refused keeps its mapping, so its address range stays taken for the rest of the run
the probe of a huge size keeps the mapping that it made, so its address range stays taken for the rest of the run
a new segment takes a record when each record is in use
a huge allocation takes a record when each record is in use
the probe of a huge size gives true when each record is in use
the probe of a large size leaves the access to its range, so the program can access storage that no allocation holds
the probe of a large size gives true when the system refuses to take the access away again
mutations.new:
libc.mprotect(cast(&h->words[at], void*), len, libc.PROT_NONE);
    return true;
